summary:
Same-sex marriage is not licensed in American Samoa. The territory's Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing in July 2015 whether the United States Supreme Court's marriage-equality ruling applied, and the Governor stated at the time that it did not, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application for a marriage licence then, and none has applied to date.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements, and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. The article sets out the litigation route: the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Reporting from the territory in July 2024 described the local ban as still treated as operative on the island and its durability under the Fourteenth Amendment as an open question, with a survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor testing the issue.

The territory's own institutions have operated on the premise that the ruling does not automatically apply. In January 2016 the Senate confirmed former Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge; at his confirmation hearing he said he had not read the Supreme Court decision, that the district court "doesn't deal with this ruling," and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change. In March 2003 the Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it; the bill's sponsor, Representative Sua Carl Schuster, wanted to preempt marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At that hearing fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing.

Birth certificates in American Samoa are altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, under a High Court ruling that the Office of Vital Statistics applies to applications from transgender individuals. The office changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Protection machinery has been used locally. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, following a June 2023 federal civil action that cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

American Samoan society is highly religious, and conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality tend to dominate. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. Against that, fa'afafine, boys raised as girls to take an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, are described in the sources as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the territory is described as tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS), formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, organises annual events and campaigns for the fa'afafine community; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei.
tangentialFactors:
A 2009 travel column described Samoan culture as tending toward traditionalism with reserved behaviour expected of people of all orientations, while characterising homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture and noting that fa'afafine are a visible part of local life. The same column described American Samoa's roughly 57,000 residents across seven islands and atolls and hotels skewed toward business travel in Pago Pago.

The 2003 legislative record shows the territory deliberately declined to enact a formal same-sex marriage ban before the 2015 federal ruling, and it documents contemporaneous local fa'afafine testimony opposing same-sex marriage on religious grounds. The January 2016 judicial confirmation exchange shows the territory's judiciary eighteen months after the ruling still operating on the premise that it did not automatically apply.

The July 2024 on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the local ban would survive a Fourteenth Amendment challenge and probed cultural dimensions bearing on the question, indicating the issue remained unresolved in territorial discourse more than a year after the federal Respect for Marriage Act took effect on 13 December 2022.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS), formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, frames its work around cultural pride and organises annual events and festivals, with beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community drawing family support. The territory's first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei.

Residents have used federal protection machinery: in September 2023 the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case with the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee, resolving a June 2023 federal civil action that had cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 federal marriage-equality ruling is legally operative in American Samoa is unresolved: official statements from 2015 said it did not apply, a 2026 law review article by local practitioners concludes it does, and reporting from July 2024 described the question as open. No same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence in the territory, so no court has ruled on the point.

The sources do not document any trans-specific violence rate for American Samoa against which the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge could be measured, and no later incident of that kind is recorded in this inventory.

Whether the Office of Vital Statistics will change a gender marker without surgery, and what documentation beyond a medical declaration it requires in practice, is not specified in the sources.
